case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Pennsylvania may constitutionally treat a foreign corporation’s registration to do business in the state as consent to general personal jurisdiction for any claim, including claims unrelated to Pennsylvania.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, Due Process Clause (personal jurisdiction limits), as applied to Pennsylvania’s corporate registration/consent-by-registration regime (and related state statutes requiring registration to do business).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that Pennsylvania can require an out-of-state corporation to consent to personal jurisdiction as a condition of doing business and that Norfolk Southern’s registration therefore constitutes valid consent to general jurisdiction, consistent with historical practice and older Supreme Court precedents recognizing jurisdiction based on express or implied consent/appointment of an in-state agent.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent argues that deeming registration to do business as consent to all-purpose (general) jurisdiction violates due process after International Shoe and Daimler because it allows suit on claims with no connection to the forum and effectively circumvents the “at home” limitation on general jurisdiction; any purported ‘consent’ extracted through mandatory registration is not genuine consent and should not create general jurisdiction.
key_precedents: Goodyear Dunlop Tires Operations, S.A. v. Brown (2011)
Pennsylvania Fire Ins. Co. of Philadelphia v. Gold Issue Mining & Milling Co. (1917)
Insurance Corp. of Ireland v. Compagnie des Bauxites de Guinée (1982)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito’s and Justice Barrett’s reliance on Insurance Corp. of Ireland and Pennsylvania Fire underscores the real force of the waiver/consent line, and I accept that International Shoe and Daimler did not expressly repudiate it. But their argument still does not answer the core due-process problem Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Jackson identify: when registration is effectively unavoidable for national firms, treating it as “consent” would allow States to legislate around Daimler’s “at home” limit and recreate universal general jurisdiction, undermining predictability and workability. Under a minimalist approach that preserves institutional legitimacy, the narrower and less disruptive course is to confine Pennsylvania Fire to its Pennoyer-era agent/service setting rather than extend it into a broad exception that would swallow our modern framework. If Commerce Clause doctrine has a role, it does not relieve us of the obligation to ensure that purported consent here is meaningfully voluntary under contemporary due process.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh offer the strongest objection: that Pennsylvania’s registration scheme is practically mandatory and would permit States to evade Daimler by relabeling compulsion as “consent.” But that argument smuggles in a novel due-process “anti-conditions” rule and treats Daimler’s contact-based limits as exclusive even where the defendant has waived the personal-jurisdiction right; Insurance Corp. of Ireland squarely characterizes personal jurisdiction as an individual due-process protection subject to waiver. Pennsylvania Fire is not merely a Pennoyer-era service/agent case; its core rationale is consent-by-statutory-condition, a historically recognized basis the Court has never repudiated in terms, and narrowing it to avoid policy consequences would amount to silent overruling inconsistent with my originalist method. If modern economic realities make States’ conditions unfair or distort interstate commerce, the more textually and historically appropriate tools are the Commerce Clause or legislative correction, not rewriting the Due Process Clause to deem clear, notice-based consent categorically involuntary.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Jackson’s “coerced/meaningful waiver” objection is the strongest point for Respondent, but it asks us to constitutionalize a new due-process anti-conditions doctrine untethered to our personal-jurisdiction cases. As Justice Kagan notes, Insurance Corp. of Ireland squarely treats personal jurisdiction as an individual due-process protection subject to waiver, and the relevant question is notice and clear statutory consequence—not whether market realities make the option unattractive. Justice Kavanaugh’s institutional concern that States will “contract around” Daimler is a serious policy worry, but Daimler and Goodyear limited nonconsensual general jurisdiction based on contacts; they did not eliminate the distinct consent-based ground recognized in Pennsylvania Fire, and “narrowing” it into a mere Pennoyer service fiction looks like silent overruling. If there is a constitutional backstop to overreaching registration conditions, it fits more naturally in the Commerce Clause or state-law constraints than in redefining due process to invalidate express statutory consent whenever doing business is important.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Jackson’s “coerced consent” point is the strongest: modern registration can be practically necessary, and we should not let States re-label their way around Daimler’s predictability concerns. But that argument still assumes Daimler supplies a nonwaivable due-process ceiling even when the defendant has accepted an explicit jurisdictional condition, and Insurance Corp. of Ireland treats personal jurisdiction as an individual right that can be waived; Pennsylvania Fire remains the closest precedent recognizing consent through a clear statutory regime. Under my pragmatic lens, the fairness safeguard is notice and clarity—if the statute unambiguously tells corporations that registration entails suit on unrelated claims, they can plan accordingly and injured plaintiffs are not left without a workable forum against nationwide actors. If Pennsylvania’s leveraging of market access becomes an interstate-burden problem, I agree with Justice Kagan that it is better addressed through Commerce Clause doctrine or legislative calibration than by creating a new Due Process anti-conditions rule that would generate indeterminate litigation over “how much” economic pressure defeats waiver.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s workability/end-run concern is the strongest point: a broad registration-equals-consent rule could invite forum shopping and pressure Daimler’s “at home” framework. But that critique assumes Daimler supplies a nonwaivable due-process ceiling even where a defendant has accepted a clearly stated jurisdictional condition; as Justice Alito and Justice Barrett emphasize, Insurance Corp. of Ireland treats personal jurisdiction as a waivable individual protection, and Pennsylvania Fire squarely recognizes consent-by-statute as an independent pathway that our later contact-based cases did not expressly displace. Justice Jackson’s “meaningful waiver”/coercion framing is intuitively appealing, yet turning due process into an anti-conditions inquiry would be a major doctrinal move lacking clear footholds in our waiver cases and would likely generate administrability problems over how much economic pressure is “too much.” If Pennsylvania Fire is to be narrowed or overruled in light of modern commerce, that should be done explicitly on stare decisis grounds; absent that, I read it as controlling on this Fourteenth Amendment question, with any broader interstate-burden concerns addressed elsewhere.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh make the strongest institutional point: a State could try to “legislate around” Daimler by deeming registration universal consent, inviting forum shopping and unpredictability. But that argument assumes Daimler’s contact-based limits are exclusive even when the defendant has waived the objection, while Pennsylvania Fire—reinforced by Insurance Corp. of Ireland’s characterization of personal jurisdiction as an individual right subject to waiver—recognizes consent as a distinct, historically grounded basis the later cases did not purport to erase. Justice Jackson’s “not meaningful”/coercion framing would require importing an anti-conditions doctrine into the Due Process Clause and turning voluntariness into an economic-necessity inquiry untethered to our waiver precedents; under an originalist/textualist approach, that is a doctrinal innovation better addressed (if at all) via the Commerce Clause or legislation. Reading Pennsylvania Fire “narrowly” simply to avoid Daimler’s consequences, as Justice Kavanaugh urges, looks like silent overruling rather than faithful stare decisis, and I cannot endorse that move on this record.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Barrett are right that Pennsylvania Fire and Insurance Corp. of Ireland recognize consent/waiver as a basis for personal jurisdiction, and I take seriously their stare decisis point. But Chief Justice Roberts correctly identifies the doctrinal and institutional problem: treating mandatory registration as all-purpose “consent” would allow States to statute around Daimler’s “at home” rule and reintroduce the forum-shopping and unpredictability Daimler sought to constrain. Under my precedent-and-workability approach, the better reconciliation is to read Pennsylvania Fire in its Pennoyer-era agent/service context and not as a modern, unlimited jurisdictional condition attached to doing ordinary interstate business; otherwise the consent label becomes an end-run that swallows our contemporary due-process limits. Justice Thomas’s suggestion that the real check is the Commerce Clause does not answer the due-process question whether this is meaningful waiver when market participation is effectively non-optional for national firms.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point is the end-run concern: that treating registration as consent would allow States to re-create universal general jurisdiction and destabilize Daimler’s predictability. But that argument presupposes Daimler supplies the due-process limit even when a defendant has waived the objection; as Justice Alito notes, Daimler and International Shoe are contact-based constraints for nonconsenting defendants, while Insurance Corp. of Ireland treats personal jurisdiction as an individual right subject to waiver and Pennsylvania Fire remains the most on-point precedent recognizing statutory consent through registration/agent appointment. Justice Jackson’s “coerced consent” framing would require importing a freestanding voluntariness/anti-conditions doctrine into the Due Process Clause, a significant doctrinal move not grounded in our consent precedents and one that would invite case-by-case litigation over economic pressure. If Pennsylvania’s scheme is problematic as a matter of interstate burdens or regulatory leverage, that is more naturally addressed under the Commerce Clause or by legislative choice, not by deeming express statutory consent categorically invalid under the Fourteenth Amendment.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Barrett are correct that Pennsylvania Fire and Insurance Corp. of Ireland preserve consent/waiver as a doctrinally distinct basis for personal jurisdiction, and that International Shoe/Daimler did not expressly overrule those cases. But that only shifts the question to what counts as meaningful waiver under modern due process: as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, a mandatory registration regime for ordinary interstate business is not a voluntary relinquishment so much as a statutory end-run that would let States recreate universal general jurisdiction and nullify Daimler’s predictable limits by relabeling. I am not adopting a free-floating “anti-conditions” doctrine; rather, I would reconcile stare decisis by reading Pennsylvania Fire narrowly in its Pennoyer-era service/agent-appointment context and declining to extend it to compelled, all-purpose jurisdiction untethered to forum connection in today’s economy. Justice Thomas’s suggestion that coercion is solely a Commerce Clause problem does not answer the due-process inquiry when the asserted “consent” lacks the voluntariness that makes waiver legitimate for an individual constitutional protection.

John Roberts.reasoning: Pennsylvania’s scheme treats a mandatory registration to do business as blanket “consent” to all-purpose jurisdiction for claims wholly unrelated to the forum, which in practical effect circumvents the Due Process limits on general jurisdiction articulated in Goodyear and Daimler (general jurisdiction ordinarily only where a corporation is “at home”). While Pennsylvania Fire (1917) involved jurisdiction predicated on an appointed agent, that pre-International Shoe framework cannot be extended to deem coerced registration a voluntary waiver of modern due-process protections, especially where the asserted jurisdiction bears no connection to Pennsylvania. Consistent with International Shoe’s insistence on fairness and the modern general-jurisdiction line, the better course for institutional legitimacy is to read Pennsylvania Fire narrowly (or as superseded in this context) and hold that registration alone does not establish general jurisdiction under the Fourteenth Amendment. Insurance Corp. of Ireland confirms that personal jurisdiction can be waived, but it does not require treating compelled compliance with a state registration statute as valid consent to universal jurisdiction.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Due Process Clause permits a defendant to waive personal-jurisdiction objections, and the Constitution’s original public meaning accommodated jurisdiction grounded in express or implied consent as a condition of doing business. This Court’s pre-International Shoe decisions sustained consent-by-registration regimes, including Pennsylvania Fire Ins. Co. v. Gold Issue Mining & Milling Co. (1917), which treated the appointment of an in-state agent under a state statute as a “voluntary act” amounting to consent to jurisdiction even for out-of-state claims. International Shoe and Daimler addressed jurisdiction based on contacts, not the separate, historically rooted basis of consent, and Insurance Corp. of Ireland confirms personal jurisdiction is an individual right subject to waiver. Because Pennsylvania’s statute makes registration the vehicle for consent, enforcing that consent is consistent with due process as historically understood, even if it would otherwise exceed the “at home” limits of general jurisdiction.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Due Process Clause permits a defendant to waive personal-jurisdiction objections, and consent remains an independent, historically grounded basis for jurisdiction. Pennsylvania Fire Ins. Co. v. Gold Issue Mining & Milling Co. (1917) squarely upheld general jurisdiction where state law conditioned doing business on appointing an in-state agent for service, and nothing in International Shoe (1945) or Daimler (2014) purported to overrule that consent-based rule. International Shoe and its progeny address jurisdiction based on contacts and fairness absent consent; they do not prohibit a State from treating registration under its statutes as assent to suit if the condition is clearly imposed. Given that Norfolk Southern registered under Pennsylvania’s regime, Insurance Corp. of Ireland (1982) confirms the constitutional validity of jurisdiction by consent/waiver, and practical consequences counsel against creating a broad new constitutional limitation that invites forum-shopping disputes over “at home” when a defendant has accepted an explicit jurisdictional condition.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Pennsylvania may treat a foreign corporation’s registration to do business—and the attendant appointment of an in-state agent for service—as consent to personal jurisdiction, and this Court’s controlling precedent in Pennsylvania Fire Ins. Co. v. Gold Issue Mining & Milling Co. (1917) squarely upheld that consent-based regime under the Fourteenth Amendment’s Due Process Clause. International Shoe and Daimler limit general jurisdiction over nonconsenting defendants based on contacts and the “at home” standard, but they do not purport to eliminate jurisdiction grounded in consent or waiver, which this Court reaffirmed as a due process concept in Insurance Corp. of Ireland v. Compagnie des Bauxites de Guinée (1982). Treating registration as consent also promotes practical access to courts for injured plaintiffs—often facing significant barriers—so long as the state has clearly conditioned doing business on that jurisdictional consequence and the corporation had notice. On this record, stare decisis and the distinct doctrinal track for consent support upholding Pennsylvania’s statute as applied.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Pennsylvania’s scheme is best understood as a consent-based ground for jurisdiction: the corporation registers and appoints an in-state agent knowing that, under state law, doing so carries jurisdictional consequences, and this Court has long treated such consent as sufficient. Pennsylvania Fire (1917) squarely upheld general jurisdiction on that basis, and International Shoe (1945) and Daimler (2014) address limits on asserting jurisdiction over nonconsenting defendants, not the separate doctrine that personal jurisdiction may be waived or conferred by consent. Insurance Corp. of Ireland (1982) reinforces that the Due Process Clause protects an individual right that can be waived, supporting the view that registration-based consent—however motivated—can be constitutionally effective. Given statutory coherence and administrability, I would follow Pennsylvania Fire absent a clear conflict and leave any policy concerns to legislatures or the Dormant Commerce Clause, not due process.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Due Process Clause permits a defendant to waive personal-jurisdiction objections, and this Court has long recognized consent-based jurisdiction as a distinct ground from minimum-contacts jurisdiction. Pennsylvania’s statute makes registration to do business—and appointment of an in-state agent for service—operate as consent, a rule this Court upheld in Pennsylvania Fire Ins. Co. v. Gold Issue Mining & Milling Co. (1917), and nothing in International Shoe or Daimler purports to overrule that consent line; those cases address jurisdiction over nonconsenting defendants. Respect for stare decisis and the separation-of-powers counsel against treating International Shoe’s judge-made minimum-contacts framework as silently invalidating a settled consent rule without this Court saying so. If there is a policy problem with States demanding consent as the price of doing business, that is a matter better addressed through legislation (and potentially the Commerce Clause) rather than by rewriting due process limits beyond their original and historical understanding.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: After International Shoe Co. v. Washington and Daimler AG v. Bauman, the Due Process Clause generally limits all-purpose jurisdiction to where a corporation is “at home,” and Pennsylvania’s consent-by-registration rule would functionally evade that constitutional limitation by forcing nationwide jurisdiction as the price of doing business. Although Pennsylvania Fire upheld a registration/agent statute as “consent” to general jurisdiction, that Pennoyer-era approach is in serious tension with the Court’s modern due-process framework and would create significant practical and workability problems by inviting forum shopping and imposing unpredictable litigation burdens on interstate commerce. Insurance Corp. of Ireland recognizes that personal jurisdiction can be waived, but “consent” extracted through mandatory registration is not the kind of voluntary, meaningful waiver that should justify general jurisdiction over claims wholly unrelated to Pennsylvania. Respecting precedent and institutional legitimacy, the better course is to read Pennsylvania Fire narrowly and adhere to Daimler’s “at home” rule for unconnected claims.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Due Process Clause permits a defendant to waive personal-jurisdiction protections by consent, and this Court has long treated appointment of an in-state agent under a registration statute—construed by the state to allow suit on any claim—as express consent to general jurisdiction. Pennsylvania Fire Ins. Co. v. Gold Issue Mining & Milling Co. upheld that regime, and neither International Shoe nor Daimler purported to overrule consent-based jurisdiction; those cases address jurisdiction grounded in contacts, not waiver. Insurance Corp. of Ireland confirms that personal jurisdiction is an individual right subject to waiver, and a State may condition the privilege of doing business on accepting service and jurisdiction on the terms its statute clearly provides. Given the continuing force of Pennsylvania Fire and the textual distinction between jurisdiction by consent and jurisdiction by minimum contacts, Pennsylvania may treat registration as consent to general jurisdiction when its law makes that consequence clear.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Pennsylvania’s consent-by-registration rule effectively converts routine compliance with a mandatory business-registration statute into all-purpose jurisdiction, producing the same practical result Daimler AG v. Bauman and Goodyear Dunlop Tires Operations, S.A. v. Brown rejected: suit on claims with no forum connection against a defendant not “at home” in the State, in tension with the Fourteenth Amendment’s Due Process Clause. While Pennsylvania Fire recognized jurisdiction based on an express statutory “consent,” modern due process doctrine after International Shoe frames jurisdictional limits around fairness and the defendant’s forum ties, and treating coerced registration as blanket consent risks eroding those procedural protections and incentivizing forum shopping. Insurance Corp. of Ireland confirms jurisdiction can be waived, but waiver must be meaningfully voluntary; conditioning access to a State’s market on surrendering a core due-process limitation is not the kind of genuine consent that should permit general jurisdiction. On balance, the more procedurally fair and workable rule is to confine general jurisdiction to “at home” fora and allow specific jurisdiction where the claims arise from Pennsylvania-related conduct.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Pennsylvania may constitutionally treat a foreign corporation’s registration to do business (and appointment of an in-state agent) as consent to general personal jurisdiction in Pennsylvania courts, even for claims unrelated to the forum.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, Due Process Clause (personal jurisdiction limits); implicated state law is Pennsylvania’s corporate registration/consent-by-registration scheme (registration to do business and designation of agent for service).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Mallory argues that Pennsylvania can require an out-of-state corporation to consent to general jurisdiction as a condition of doing business in the Commonwealth, and that this form of consent-based jurisdiction is consistent with longstanding Supreme Court precedent recognizing jurisdiction by consent (including consent inferred from corporate registration statutes). He contends that modern ‘at home’ limits on general jurisdiction (e.g., Daimler) regulate non-consensual general jurisdiction, not situations where a corporation knowingly accepts a statutory bargain to register and thereby submit to suit in the forum.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Norfolk Southern argues that treating routine registration to do business as consent to all-purpose (general) jurisdiction violates due process because it is not genuine, voluntary consent and would effectively reinstate universal general jurisdiction in any state where a corporation registers. It maintains that modern due process doctrine (International Shoe and Daimler) limits general jurisdiction to where a corporation is ‘at home’ (typically incorporation and principal place of business), and that a state cannot circumvent those limits by deeming mandatory business registration to be consent—especially where the statute does not clearly provide notice that registration equals consent to general jurisdiction.
key_precedents: International Shoe Co. v. Washington, 326 U.S. 310 (1945)
Goodyear Dunlop Tires Operations, S.A. v. Brown, 564 U.S. 915 (2011)
Insurance Corp. of Ireland v. Compagnie des Bauxites de Guinée, 456 U.S. 694 (1982)
Pennsylvania Fire Ins. Co. v. Gold Issue Mining & Milling Co., 243 U.S. 93 (1917)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito’s and Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point is doctrinal: Daimler/Goodyear speak to nonconsensual general jurisdiction, and Pennsylvania Fire plus Insurance Corp. of Ireland preserve consent/waiver as a distinct path. But that does not resolve what counts as “consent” for due-process purposes today; treating mandatory, routine registration as blanket consent would—just as Justice Kavanaugh emphasizes—invite States to legislate around Daimler and re-create near-universal general jurisdiction, destabilizing our settled framework and undermining predictability. I do not think Pennsylvania Fire can bear that weight after International Shoe’s architecture; as a minimalist matter we should read it narrowly to true, express submission to suit, not a statutory fiction attached to market access. Justice Thomas’s originalist account is serious, but it would require us to accept an end-run around modern due-process limits without an explicit overruling or a limiting principle, and I am not prepared to do that on this record.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh press the strongest point—that consent-by-registration permits an “end-run around Daimler”—but that is a policy/institutional objection that cannot silently rewrite the Due Process Clause’s original meaning or erase a historically accepted consent category. Daimler and Goodyear, by their terms, constrain nonconsensual general jurisdiction; they do not purport to eliminate waiver/consent, and Insurance Corp. of Ireland reinforces that personal jurisdiction is an individual due-process protection that can be waived with adequate notice. Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s “not meaningfully voluntary” theory imports modern economic-compulsion concepts that are difficult to ground in the original public meaning, given the widespread 19th-century practice of conditioning in-state business on appointment of an agent and amenability to suit. If States are exploiting that mechanism to impose excessive interstate burdens, that concern is better addressed through the Commerce Clause or unconstitutional-conditions principles, not by extending Daimler beyond its nonconsensual framework to overrule Pennsylvania Fire sub silentio.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The strongest respondent point is Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s “end-run around Daimler” concern, but that is a structural/policy objection to the consequences of consent-by-registration, not a due-process reason to deny that consent is categorically sufficient when clearly given. Daimler and Goodyear cabin nonconsensual general jurisdiction; as Justice Barrett and Justice Thomas emphasize, they do not purport to displace the separate consent/waiver track reaffirmed in Insurance Corp. of Ireland, and Pennsylvania Fire directly upheld a statute that treated registration/agent appointment as consent. Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson’s voluntariness critique asks us to constitutionalize a modern economic-coercion inquiry into “consent,” but our waiver doctrine generally turns on notice and the defendant’s choice to accept the legal consequence, leaving interstate-burden objections to the Commerce Clause or unconstitutional-conditions doctrines rather than rewriting Due Process. Absent an express overruling, I do not see a principled, doctrinally grounded basis to narrow Pennsylvania Fire to the point of ineffectiveness simply to protect Daimler’s policy equilibrium.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito’s and Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point is doctrinal: Daimler/Goodyear speak to nonconsensual jurisdiction, and Pennsylvania Fire plus Insurance Corp. of Ireland recognize waiver/consent as a separate track. But that only moves the inquiry to whether Pennsylvania has extracted a meaningful waiver or imposed a compelled fiction—because treating mandatory, economy-wide registration as blanket “consent” would, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, let States nullify Daimler’s fairness and predictability limits by statute. Justice Thomas’s historical practice argument is important, yet due process in our modern framework is not indifferent to practical coercion and real-world burdens on defendants and litigants; a label of “consent” cannot do all the work when the condition is functionally unavoidable and untethered to the forum or the claims. I therefore would read Pennsylvania Fire narrowly and require truly express, deliberate consent (not presumed from ministerial compliance) to preserve both waiver doctrine and the integrity of our modern jurisdictional architecture.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh raise the hardest point: if registration automatically equals blanket consent, States can effectively legislate around Daimler/Goodyear and recreate universal general jurisdiction. But that objection, as a doctrinal matter, targets the wisdom of the regime rather than its due-process validity where the State has made the jurisdictional consequence unmistakably clear; Daimler and Goodyear constrain nonconsensual all-purpose jurisdiction and do not purport to displace the separate waiver/consent track reaffirmed in Insurance Corp. of Ireland and applied in Pennsylvania Fire. Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s “not meaningfully voluntary” critique is powerful in real-world terms, yet importing economic-compulsion notions into Due Process consent would be an unstable, hard-to-administer revision of our waiver cases and would effectively narrow Pennsylvania Fire sub silentio rather than confronting it directly. The more workable, coherent middle ground is to enforce consent-by-registration only when the statute clearly ties registration/agent appointment to amenability to suit, leaving broader coercion or interstate-burden concerns to Commerce Clause or unconstitutional-conditions analysis.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh offer the strongest objection: that consent-by-registration would permit an end-run around Daimler/Goodyear and recreate near-universal general jurisdiction. But that concern goes to the wisdom of broad registration statutes, not to whether the Due Process Clause disables a historically recognized, waiver-based ground of jurisdiction that Pennsylvania Fire upheld and that Insurance Corp. of Ireland reaffirms as doctrinally distinct from minimum-contacts limits on nonconsensual jurisdiction, as Justice Thomas emphasizes. Reading Daimler to silently displace consent would be methodologically unsound: those cases did not address consent and our stare decisis rules do not permit sub silentio overruling. If States are exploiting registration conditions in ways that burden interstate commerce, that is better policed through the Commerce Clause or unconstitutional-conditions principles—not by redefining “consent” in due process to avoid Daimler’s practical consequences.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Gorsuch press the strongest point that Daimler/Goodyear address nonconsensual jurisdiction and that Pennsylvania Fire plus Insurance Corp. of Ireland preserve waiver as a distinct doctrinal route. But that framing does not resolve whether Pennsylvania’s registration scheme amounts to a meaningful, voluntary relinquishment as opposed to a compelled legal fiction attached to a ministerial prerequisite for ordinary market access—an institutional concern Chief Justice Roberts rightly emphasizes because it would allow States to legislate an end-run around Daimler and recreate near-universal general jurisdiction in practice. Justice Thomas’s historical account is relevant, yet I read Pennsylvania Fire narrowly in light of the post-International Shoe due-process architecture: it cannot be extended to treat mandatory registration, without genuinely express and deliberate consent to suit on unrelated claims, as blanket consent today. Absent that limiting principle, the consent label would swallow our modern predictability and fairness doctrine and destabilize settled expectations, which weighs heavily under my precedent- and institution-focused approach.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point is the structural “end-run around Daimler” concern, but that objection targets limits on nonconsensual general jurisdiction and does not supply a Due Process rule that negates a distinct, historically recognized consent pathway. As Justice Thomas and Justice Alito emphasize, Insurance Corp. of Ireland treats personal jurisdiction as an individual due-process protection that can be waived, and Pennsylvania Fire—never expressly overruled—upheld a statute that made registration/agent appointment the predicate for amenability; under an originalist and stare decisis approach, we should not narrow that holding sub silentio to harmonize with later cases that did not address consent. Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s “coercion” framing is intuitively appealing, but it imports an economic-voluntariness test that is hard to derive from the Due Process Clause’s original public meaning or our waiver doctrine, and it would functionally rewrite consent out of the jurisdictional framework. If States’ market-access conditions are thought excessive, that is more coherently addressed through other constitutional constraints (e.g., Commerce Clause/unconstitutional conditions) rather than expanding Daimler beyond its text and reasoning to erase consent-by-registration.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Gorsuch are right that Pennsylvania Fire and Insurance Corp. of Ireland preserve consent/waiver as a distinct doctrinal path, but that framing does not resolve whether Pennsylvania’s “consent” is a real, voluntary relinquishment of a due-process protection or a compelled fiction attached to a ministerial act required for ordinary market access. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh correctly warn that treating routine registration as blanket consent would let States manufacture near-universal general jurisdiction and functionally undo Daimler/Goodyear’s fairness and predictability constraints—an outcome due process, understood pragmatically and in light of practical consequences, should not tolerate. Justice Thomas’s historical practice point is substantial, but it does not persuade me to extend a pre-International Shoe “presence” regime into today’s national economy where the asserted waiver is neither targeted nor meaningfully choiceful. Ireland supports enforcing truly express, deliberate consent; it does not require us to deem coerced, across-the-board “consent” sufficient for unrelated claims.

John Roberts.reasoning: Pennsylvania’s effort to treat routine registration to do business and appointment of an agent as consent to all-purpose jurisdiction risks collapsing the Due Process limits on general jurisdiction recognized in Goodyear and Daimler, effectively recreating nationwide general jurisdiction wherever a corporation registers. While Pennsylvania Fire upheld a consent-by-registration regime, that 1917 decision rested on a now-superseded conception of corporate “presence” and predates International Shoe’s framework, under which jurisdictional assertions must be consistent with “traditional notions of fair play and substantial justice.” Absent a clear, genuinely voluntary, and narrowly tailored consent, Pennsylvania cannot evade Daimler’s “at home” constraint through a statutory deeming rule; protecting institutional legitimacy counsels adhering to the modern doctrinal line and rejecting this end-run. Accordingly, due process under the Fourteenth Amendment bars Pennsylvania from asserting general jurisdiction over claims unrelated to the forum on this basis alone.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Due Process Clause permits personal jurisdiction based on a defendant’s consent, and at the Founding and throughout the Fourteenth Amendment’s ratification era, States commonly conditioned a foreign corporation’s right to do business on appointment of an in-state agent to accept service and submission to suit. This Court upheld that arrangement as a “voluntary act” consistent with due process in Pennsylvania Fire Ins. Co. v. Gold Issue Mining & Milling Co., 243 U.S. 93 (1917), and nothing in the Fourteenth Amendment’s text eliminates consent as an independent ground of jurisdiction. International Shoe and Daimler address judge-made limits on nonconsensual jurisdiction keyed to “minimum contacts” and being “at home,” but they do not overrule the longstanding consent-by-registration line recognized in cases such as Insurance Corp. of Ireland v. Compagnie des Bauxites de Guinée, 456 U.S. 694 (1982). Because Pennsylvania’s scheme rests on consent rather than coercive assertions of adjudicatory power, it is constitutionally permissible under the original public meaning of due process.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Pennsylvania’s statute expressly conditions the privilege of doing business on a foreign corporation’s registration and appointment of an in-state agent, and longstanding doctrine treats such compliance as consent to suit—a traditional basis of personal jurisdiction independent of minimum-contacts analysis. Pennsylvania Fire Ins. Co. v. Gold Issue Mining & Milling Co. (1917) squarely upheld general jurisdiction on that consent-by-registration theory, and neither International Shoe nor Daimler purported to overrule that rule because those cases address nonconsensual assertions of general jurisdiction. Treating registration as consent also has practical benefits for orderly service of process and predictable litigation, and due process does not forbid a State from attaching reasonable jurisdictional consequences to the choice to conduct business within its borders. If there are concerns about undue burdens on interstate commerce, they are more naturally analyzed under the Commerce Clause than by expanding the Due Process Clause to invalidate a form of consent this Court has long recognized.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Pennsylvania’s scheme effectively converts the ordinary, often mandatory act of registering to do business and appointing an agent for service into all-purpose jurisdiction for any claim anywhere, a result in tension with the Due Process Clause’s fairness limits on general jurisdiction articulated in International Shoe and reaffirmed in Goodyear and Daimler (general jurisdiction ordinarily lies only where a corporation is “at home”). Treating such registration as “consent” is not meaningfully voluntary in today’s economy and would allow states to circumvent Daimler’s constraint by attaching a sweeping jurisdictional penalty to market access, with harsh practical impacts on plaintiffs and defendants alike through forum shopping and litigation costs. While Pennsylvania Fire recognized consent-by-registration in 1917, that rule sits uneasily with modern due process doctrine and should not be extended to sustain a regime that recreates near-universal general jurisdiction. The better course is to require either true, express consent or jurisdiction tied to the forum-related contacts and fairness considerations that International Shoe demands.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Pennsylvania’s exercise of jurisdiction rests on a consent theory: by registering to do business and appointing an in-state agent under Pennsylvania’s scheme, a foreign corporation can be treated as having accepted jurisdictional consequences that are analytically distinct from the “at home” limits on nonconsensual general jurisdiction in Goodyear and Daimler. Pennsylvania Fire held that a state may condition doing business on such consent and that service on the appointed agent suffices, and International Shoe’s fairness framework and Daimler’s narrowing of general jurisdiction do not squarely overrule that consent-based holding because they address jurisdiction absent consent. Insurance Corp. of Ireland confirms that personal jurisdiction is a waivable due-process protection and may be established by consent, supporting the view that consent-by-registration—so long as the statute provides clear notice—can satisfy the Fourteenth Amendment Due Process Clause. Given stare decisis and the availability of narrowing constructions (e.g., requiring clear statutory notice and treating consent as a deliberate waiver), I would uphold Pennsylvania’s approach here rather than extend Daimler to silently displace Pennsylvania Fire.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Due Process Clause permits personal jurisdiction by consent, and Pennsylvania’s statute—on its face—treats registration to do business and appointment of an agent for service as a form of consent to suit, bringing this case within the traditional category of waiver recognized in Insurance Corp. of Ireland v. Compagnie des Bauxites. Pennsylvania Fire Ins. Co. v. Gold Issue Mining & Milling Co. upheld exactly that arrangement, and International Shoe and Daimler address the limits on nonconsensual jurisdiction grounded in contacts and fairness, not situations where a defendant has consented. Absent a clear overruling of Pennsylvania Fire, stare decisis and the separation-of-powers concern with judicially revising jurisdictional rules counsel applying that precedent as written. Any remaining ambiguity about the wisdom of such regimes is better addressed through state law reform or other constitutional doctrines (e.g., Commerce Clause), not by expanding Daimler beyond its terms.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Pennsylvania’s consent-by-registration theory effectively restores all-purpose jurisdiction in any State where a corporation must register to do business, which is in substantial tension with this Court’s modern due process framework limiting general jurisdiction to where a corporation is “at home.” See Daimler AG v. Bauman, 571 U.S. 117 (2014); Goodyear Dunlop Tires Operations, S.A. v. Brown, 564 U.S. 915 (2011). While jurisdiction can be waived or consented to, Insurance Corp. of Ireland recognizes consent as a due-process concept grounded in meaningful choice; treating routine, mandatory registration and appointment of an agent as blanket consent for unrelated suits is not a workable or realistic form of voluntary consent under the Fourteenth Amendment. Pennsylvania Fire (1917) predates International Shoe and, at minimum, should be read narrowly so it does not allow States to circumvent Daimler’s limits on general jurisdiction through a legal fiction of “consent” attached to compulsory registration.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Due Process Clause permits a defendant to waive its personal-jurisdiction objection, and this Court has long recognized jurisdiction by consent. Pennsylvania Fire Ins. Co. v. Gold Issue Mining & Milling Co., 243 U.S. 93 (1917), held that a State may, consistent with due process, treat a foreign corporation’s registration and appointment of an in-state agent as consent to suit, including on claims unrelated to the forum; nothing in the Fourteenth Amendment’s text precludes such consent. Modern decisions like International Shoe and Daimler address the constitutional limits on asserting jurisdiction over an unconsenting defendant, and they do not purport to overrule consent-based jurisdiction; Insurance Corp. of Ireland confirms that personal jurisdiction is a waivable due process right. Given Pennsylvania Fire’s direct applicability and the lack of a clear conflict with later precedent, stare decisis and methodological consistency counsel adhering to it here.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Pennsylvania’s scheme treats routine, effectively mandatory corporate registration as blanket “consent” to all-purpose jurisdiction, which is not the kind of voluntary waiver contemplated by the Due Process Clause and Insurance Corp. of Ireland v. Compagnie des Bauxites de Guinée. Under International Shoe and Daimler, general jurisdiction is ordinarily limited to where a corporation is “at home,” and allowing States to convert ministerial registration into general jurisdiction would, as a practical matter, recreate near-universal jurisdiction and undermine those limits. Pennsylvania Fire’s consent-by-registration holding arose in a different due process era and cannot be extended to permit coerced, non-bargained-for consent that defeats modern fairness and predictability concerns. Procedural fairness and notice also weigh against jurisdiction where the claim is unrelated to the forum and the “consent” is imposed as a condition of doing business rather than meaningfully chosen.
